profile.name: Korean dance
profile.tagline: From ancient shamanic nature rites to vibrant court and folk traditions.
profile.insight: Rooted in ancient shamanic nature rites, Korean dance conceals the performer's feet beneath billowing silk hanbok while fluid motions mirror traditional drums and flutes.
profile.profile: Korean traditional dance originated in ancient shamanistic rituals thousands of years ago, later receiving regular support from the royal court during the Goryeo and Joseon dynasties. Performance styles range from stately court jeongjae and masked folk dances to meditative ritual movements and newly created traditional forms like the fan dance. Dancers follow curvilinear paths with little short-term repetition, their legs and feet entirely concealed by billowing traditional hanbok. The music upholds the dance, while the dancer serves as the physical embodiment of traditional drums, flutes, and percussion.
profile.profile_long: Dance in Korea began with shamanistic early rituals five thousand years ago and now ranges from folk dance to newly created and adopted contemporary dance. By the time of the later Korean kingdoms, Goryeo and Joseon, in the 2nd millennium AD, Korean traditional dance benefited from regular support of the royal court, numerous academies, and even an official ministry of the government. A number of different dances gained permanent high status, including the hermit dance, the ghost dance, buchaechum, sengmu, and the oudong, despite many having humble origins. For example, the fan dance is believed to have originated with shamans performing nature rites with leaves but evolved into one of the most highly refined Korean dances. Other Korean dances remained and remain to this day under the ambit of farmers and folk dance groups. Props used in the dances include the long billowing silk scarf of pure white used in the salpuri dance, drums, hats, swords, and fans. The themes of support for these dances may be peripheral or central to the story of the dance. In the ghost dance, the entertainer has a joyous reunion with a deceased spouse, only to endure the heartbreak of reseparation. Due to cultural suppression by Imperial Japan, most dance academies died out and some dances were lost, but pioneering dancers such as Choi Seung-hee created new forms based on traditional dances and kept traditions alive. Today, Korean traditional dance enjoys a vibrant resurgence, taught in numerous universities where top dancers are recognized as Living National Treasures. Korean traditional dance shares similarities with contemporary and lyrical forms. Moves follow a curvilinear path with little short term repetition, and the dancer's legs and feet are often entirely concealed by billowing hanbok. Emotional attributes include both somberness and joy as the dancer embodies fluid motion that surges through traditional music.

sections.origins_and_history: Dance in Korea began with shamanistic early rituals five thousand years ago and benefited from royal court support during the Goryeo and Joseon dynasties, surviving cultural suppression under Imperial Japan through the efforts of pioneering artists.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Moves follow a curvilinear path with little short term repetition. The dancer's legs and feet are often entirely concealed by billowing Hanbok, and the dancer embodies fluid motion driven by traditional music.
sections.music_and_instruments: Korean traditional music includes traditional drums, flutes, and ivory clappers. The music upholds the dance, and the dancer acts as the physical tool that shows the music in physical form.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear billowing Hanbok that entirely conceal their legs and feet, utilizing props such as long billowing white silk scarves of pure white, drums, hats, swords, and fans.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Jeongjae court dances were performed for the royal family, court officials, foreign envoys, or state-sponsored festive occasions, while folk dances were performed during village celebrations and agricultural rites.
sections.notable_figures: Choi Seung-hee created new forms of Korean dances based on traditional dances, and Kim Sook-ja is an official holder and practitioner of salpuri originating in shamanic rituals.
sections.regional_variants: Court dances are divided into Hyangak jeongjae (indigenous Korean) and Dangak jeongjae (derived from Tang China). Folk traditions include regional mask dances like Talchum and Bukcheong sajanoreum.
sections.lineage: The lineages of dance and dancers may be traced back several generations through officially recognized Living National Treasures charged with passing their dances to students.

profile.sacred_note: Many dances originated in ancient shamanistic rituals, Buddhist practices, or Confucian rites and retain sacred dimensions.
